name: Mithraism
areas: the cult's centre; Rome may have had not less than 680 mithraea
the only mithraeum in Palestine, at Caesarea Maritima
the cult's eastern reach in Europe
only three mithraea, as far east as Dura-Europos
routes: To the Danube, where a centurion makes the earliest military dedication (before 114)
To the northern frontier of Britain (140)
Carried to Syria by soldiers and merchants
marks: The cult appears to have had its centre here, where an altar to Sol Invictus Mithras of about 80–100 CE and the earliest bull-slaying monument were found.
The only mithraeum in Palestine, among the cult's earliest places (c. 80–120 CE); its ceiling keeps traces of blue paint.
The earliest military inscription to Mithras, by a centurion of the Fifteenth Legion, probably before 114.
Two altars to Mithras of 140 CE, believed to come from the empire's most northerly temple of Mithras.
A bronze plaque listed the initiates year by year and records a festival of commemoration on 26 June 184.
An ordeal pit of the early 3rd century was identified in its mithraeum.
Votive coins from Gallienus to Theodosius I show the mithraeum in use until near the end of the 4th century, when it was destroyed.
notes: Mithraic temples appear suddenly in the last quarter of the 1st century CE, in Rome, on the Rhine and Danube and at Caesarea Maritima; Statius mentions Mithras in a cave about 80 CE.
A centurion of the Fifteenth Legion dedicates an altar to Mithras at Carnuntum on the Danube, probably before 114, the earliest military inscription.
Altars to Mithras are set up at Inveresk in Scotland (140 CE), believed to be the empire's most northerly temple of Mithras.
Late in the reign of Antoninus Pius and under Marcus Aurelius the mysteries make their first important expansion, with all their key elements in place.
In the 2nd and 3rd centuries Mithraism reaches the height of its popularity, spreading at an “astonishing” rate among soldiers, merchants and officials.
By the later 3rd century the initiation ordeals are less severe, and ordeal pits are floored over.
In the 4th century Mithraists face persecution from Christians, though senators of the pagan revival still list Mithras among their cults.
Coins at Sarrebourg run to the reign of Theodosius I (379–395); by the end of the century the cult is suppressed, though it may linger in the Alps and Vosges.
src: Maarten J. Vermaseren, Corpus Inscriptionum et Monumentorum Religionis Mithriacae
Franz Cumont, Textes et monuments figurés relatifs aux mystères de Mithra (1894–1900)
